sources.name: NOAA GEFS operational archive on AWS Open Data (s3://noaa-gefs-pds)
sources.what_it_provides: THE single artefact that closes the perfect-foresight gap. Verified by direct S3 calls, no credentials: GET https://noaa-gefs-pds.s3.amazonaws.com/?list-type=2&prefix=gefs.20211015/00/atmos/pgrb2sp25/&max-keys=1000 returns 1000+ keys including gep01..gep30 .t00z.pgrb2s.0p25.f000 .. .f240 (verified gep30 present; max forecast hour 240; 3-hourly steps). The .idx sidecar for gep01.t00z.pgrb2s.0p25.f024 lists record 16 as '16:8942680:d=2021101500:APCP:surface:18-24 hour acc fcst:ENS=+1'. A byte-range GET (curl -r 8942680-9211235) on that file returned HTTP 206, 268556 bytes, magic bytes 'GRIB' - i.e. you can pull one 30-member precipitation field for one lead hour for ~270 kB per member without downloading the whole archive. Bucket root listing starts at gefs.20170101/. Gives 30 perturbed members + control + mean at 0.25 deg, 4 cycles/day (00/06/12/18z), out to 240 h.
sources.relevance: high - this is the only free, verified route to a genuine 30-member ENSEMBLE rainfall forecast valid over the Periyar for October 2021. AquaSync can replay its flagship case study driving the SCS-CN/Muskingum chain from each of 30 members issued at 00z on each day of the event, run the existing exhaustive policy search on the resulting inflow ensemble, and report what fraction of the perfect-foresight benefit survives. Every other free ensemble source checked either has no 2021 archive or no members.

sources.license: US Government public domain / NOAA open data, no registration
sources.last_activity: live operational stream, bucket updated continuously; verified 2026-08-27
sources.download_hint: List: https://noaa-gefs-pds.s3.amazonaws.com/?list-type=2&prefix=gefs.YYYYMMDD/00/atmos/pgrb2sp25/&max-keys=1000 . Fetch the .idx text file for the member+lead you want, find the APCP:surface line, take its byte offset and the next line's offset, then HTTP Range GET that slice and decode with cfgrib/eccodes or wgrib2. For the Idukki/Idamalayar catchments you need only ~4 grid cells (0.25 deg), so a whole 30-member x 10-day x 15-issue-date Oct 2021 hindcast is a few hundred MB of range reads, not TB. Longer leads: the 0.5 deg stream gefs.20211015/00/atmos/pgrb2ap5/ also exists for Oct 2021, running to f840 (35 days), and its .idx confirms 'APCP:surface:234-240 hour acc fcst:ENS=+1' at f240 - use 0p25/pgrb2sp25 to day 10 and fall back to 0p50/pgrb2ap5 only if you need leads beyond that.
sources.caveat: APCP in pgrb2s is an ACCUMULATION over a 6 h window (labelled e.g. '18-24 hour acc fcst') - you must difference/assemble correctly, not treat it as an instantaneous rate. 0.25 deg (~28 km) badly under-resolves Western Ghats orographic rainfall, so members will be biased low over the escarpment; bias-correct against IMD 0.25 deg gridded rainfall or the SLDC-derived observed inflow before feeding the SCS-CN model. GEFSv12 became operational 2020-09-23, so Oct 2021 is v12 - consistent with today's model, which is good for skill transferability.

sources.name: CAMELS-IND v2.2 (Zenodo record 14999580)
sources.what_it_provides: Verified by reading the ZIP central directory over HTTP range requests rather than downloading the 350 MB archive. It DOES exist and it DOES cover the Periyar. CWC basin 15 ('West flowing rivers from Tadri to Kanyakumari') contributes 32 of the 472 catchments, gauge ids 15001-15032, of which ~21 are physically inside Kerala. Three are on the Periyar system: 15021 Neeleswaram (10.1833 N, 76.5000 E, 4234 km2, mean elev 930.3 m, streamflow available 94.57% of 1980-2020, in the streamflow-sufficient subset with its own column in streamflow_timeseries/streamflow_observed.csv); 15031 Vandiperiyar (9.5733 N, 77.0908 E, 712 km2, mean elev 1132 m, 43.51% availability - the upstream headwater gauge nearest Idukki); 15005 Arangaly on the Periyar/Chalakudy (1342 km2, 93.58%). Neighbours also present: Bharathapuzha x4, Pamba x3, Muvattupuzha x2, Chalakudy, Chaliyar, Meenachil. Each catchment ships catchment_mean_forcings/<id>.csv with daily 1980-01-01 to 2020-12-31, 19 variables (IMD prcp/tmax/tmin, IMDAA radiation/wind/RH/evaporation/4-layer soil moisture, PET, GLEAM PET/AET), plus 8 attribute tables (name/topo/clim/hydro/land/soil/geol/anth) and per-basin shapefiles.
sources.relevance: high - directly contradicts the plausible assumption that Indian large-sample hydrology skips Kerala. 41 years of daily observed discharge at the Periyar basin outlet, with matched IMD forcings, is enough to train a single-basin or regionally-pooled LSTM inflow model and, more importantly, to give AquaSync an independent physical check on its SCS-CN + Muskingum chain. Neeleswaram (4234 km2) is the whole-basin outlet DOWNSTREAM of both Idukki and Idamalayar, so it is a regulated series, not reservoir inflow; Vandiperiyar (712 km2) is the upstream unregulated headwater gauge and is the one that is hydrologically comparable to Idukki's own catchment.
sources.http_status: 200 (ESSD article and PDF); Zenodo API 200 with a full Chrome UA + 'Accept: application/json' but 403 with a plain 'Mozilla/5.0' UA - mark 403-bot-blocked for naive curl; the record JSON and file listing were retrieved successfully and the zip serves 'accept-ranges: bytes' (HTTP 206 on Range).
sources.last_activity: v2.2 published 2025-03-13, record updated 2025-04-25 (4 versions since 2024-05)
sources.download_hint: Use v2.2 = 10.5281/zenodo.14999580, NOT the v2.1 DOI 10.5281/zenodo.14005378 cited in the ESSD paper. Files: CAMELS_IND_All_Catchments.zip (350,754,048 B), CAMELS_IND_Catchments_Streamflow_Sufficient.zip (178,141,731 B, 243 catchments), 00_CAMELS_IND_Data_Description.pdf. Zenodo's API only serves files for the LATEST version, which is why /api/records/14005378/files returns 403 while /api/records/14999580/files returns 200.
sources.caveat: CRITICAL: the v2.2 changelog states it made 'corrections to the gauge_id mapping for basin codes 12 and 15'. Basin 15 is exactly the Kerala basin. Gauge ids from v2.1 (the version the ESSD paper cites) may not match v2.2 for these catchments - if you cite a Periyar gauge id, cite the v2.2 DOI. Also: the dataset has NO state attribute, so 'in Kerala' is a geographic judgement from lat/lon, not a dataset field. And streamflow is India-WRIS/CWC gauge data, which for a heavily regulated basin reflects dam releases, not natural runoff.

sources.name: NeuralHydrology (Kratzert et al., JKU Linz)
sources.what_it_provides: GitHub API: 572 stars, 275 forks, 7 open issues, BSD-3-Clause, created 2020-09-30, last push 2026-08-09, latest release v1.13.0 (2026-01-14). PyTorch, config-YAML-driven so you train without touching code. modelzoo/ contains 25 files: cudalstm, customlstm, ealstm, embcudalstm, mclstm, mtslstm, odelstm, arlstm, gru, transformer, mamba, x_lstm, shm, hybridmodel, plus FOUR forecast-specific architectures (handoff_forecast_lstm, sequential_forecast_lstm, stacked_forecast_lstm, multihead_forecast_lstm). head.py exposes probabilistic heads: 'regression', 'gmm', 'umal', 'cmal'. datasetzoo/ contains camelsaus, camelsbr, camelscl, camelsde, camelsgb, camelsind, camelsus, caravan, hourlycamelsus, lamah AND genericdataset.py.
sources.relevance: high - two decisive details for AquaSync. (1) datasetzoo/camelsind.py means CAMELS-IND (and therefore the Periyar gauges) is a first-class supported dataset, no adapter to write. (2) genericdataset.py plus the CMAL/UMAL/GMM heads means you can train on your own single-basin SLDC inflow series and get a PROBABILISTIC inflow output - a predictive distribution, not a point forecast - which is exactly the object the policy search needs to consume once perfect foresight is removed. The forecast_lstm family separates a hindcast sequence (past observed forcing) from a forecast sequence (NWP forcing), which is the correct architecture for driving from GEFS members.
sources.download_hint: pip install neuralhydrology, or git clone + pip install -e .  Then 'nh-run train --config-file config.yml'. Tutorials at neuralhydrology.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/ cover: Data Prerequisites, Introduction, Adding a New Model (GRU), Adding a New Dataset (CAMELS-CL), Multi-Timescale Prediction, Inspecting LSTM internals, Finetuning.
sources.caveat: Single-basin training with ~20-40 years of daily data is mechanically supported but is NOT where LSTM rainfall-runoff gets its advantage - the Kratzert et al. HESS 2019 result (doi 10.5194/hess-23-5089-2019) is that a model trained on MANY basins beats per-basin calibration, and single-basin LSTMs routinely underperform a well-calibrated conceptual model. For AquaSync the defensible framing is: pool the ~32 CAMELS-IND basin-15 catchments (or all 472) to train, then fine-tune on the Periyar gauges - not train a lone LSTM on Idukki. I did NOT find any documented statement of CPU vs GPU training time in the docs, so do not quote one.

sources.name: GRRR - Google Runoff Reanalysis & Reforecast (public GCS bucket gs://flood-forecasting)
sources.what_it_provides: A second, independent, and in some ways better route to a lead-time-resolved October 2021 inflow hindcast for the Periyar - and it needs no key, no waitlist and no credentials. The Colab linked from the research site simply points at an anonymously readable GCS bucket (storage_options=dict(token="anon")) at gs://flood-forecasting/hydrologic_predictions/model_id_8583a5c2_v0/. Zarr metadata read directly over HTTPS (all 200): reanalysis/streamflow.zarr is [1,031,646 gauges x 16,063 days] contiguous 1980-01-01 to 2023-12-23; reforecast/streamflow.zarr is [1,031,646 gauges x 2,738 issue times x 8 lead times] contiguous 2016-01-01 to 2023-06-30 with lead times 0-7 days; return_periods.zarr carries 2/5/7/10/15/20/25/50/100/200-year thresholds per gauge; hybas_outlet_locations_UNOFFICIAL.zarr gives 1,034,083 gauge_id/latitude/longitude triples. KERALA AND THE PERIYAR ARE COVERED - all 16 lat/lon chunks were downloaded and analysed: 589 virtual gauges fall inside the Kerala bbox (8.2-12.8 N, 74.8-77.4 E), 588 of them present in the reanalysis index; 96 fall inside the Periyar catchment box (9.6-10.6 N, 76.1-77.35 E); and the nearest gauge to Idukki dam is hybas_4121152880 at 9.8396 N, 76.9729 E - 0.61 km away. Its actual reanalysis timeseries was pulled and it reproduces the August 2018 Kerala flood: 2018-08-13 80.67, 08-14 136.53, 08-15 227.69, 08-16 239.65 (peak), 08-17 190.54 m3/s, against its own return-period thresholds of 173.2 (2-yr), 214.9 (5-yr) and 242.2 (10-yr) m3/s - i.e. the model places that event between a 5- and 10-year flood at Idukki.
sources.relevance: high - this is the second pillar of the fix and it is complementary to GEFS rather than redundant. GEFS gives error-bearing RAINFALL that AquaSync pushes through its own SCS-CN/Muskingum chain; GRRR gives error-bearing DISCHARGE straight out of a global ML model, at 0-7 day lead (lead 0 is the REANALYSIS value, driven by observed CPC/IMERG rainfall, not a forecast - Google's own docs give the identity Reanalysis[T] == Reforecast[T+1, lead=0]; score benefit retention from lead 1 upward or perfect-foresight leaks back in), on a virtual gauge 610 m from Idukki dam, covering the whole of October 2021. Running both separates two questions the project currently cannot distinguish: how much benefit is lost because the RAINFALL forecast is wrong, versus how much is lost because the rainfall-runoff model is wrong. The return_periods array also supplies a ready-made, externally-defined severity scale for the case study.

sources.caveat: THREE things to state honestly if this is used. (1) It is a REFORECAST, not the forecast issued in October 2021 - a modern model re-run over past dates, free of the 2021-vintage operational model's deficiencies, so it will flatter the result relative to what an operator actually had. GEFS operational (which IS what existed) is the stricter test; use GRRR as the upper-middle case and say so explicitly. (2) The gauges are HydroBASINS level-12 VIRTUAL outlets, not physical gauges - hybas_4121152880 is a modelled point near the dam, not a measured inflow, and it has never been calibrated against Idukki observations. Validate it against the SLDC inflow scrape before trusting it. (3) The notebook prose says the reforecast covers '2016-2022' while the actual time axis runs to 2023-06-30 - trust the axis, not the prose.

sources.name: OpenHydroNet - google-research/flood-forecasting (the open-sourced Flood Hub models)
sources.what_it_provides: GitHub API: 328 stars, 81 forks, 14 open issues, Apache-2.0, created 2025-09-29, last push 2026-08-25. README states it is 'a fork of NeuralHydrology, heavily modified and extended to support forecast sequences using the specific model architectures that are used operationally in the Google FloodHub', and explicitly 'This is not an officially supported Google product'. Two model implementations: Mean-Embedding-Forecast-LSTM (marked 'Current production model (as of December 2025) for Google FloodHub', reference Gauch et al., HESS 29, 6221, 2025, doi 10.5194/hess-29-6221-2025) and Handoff-Forecast-LSTM. Package name googlehydrology; entry point 'run train|evaluate|infer --config-file'. Ships example-configs/floodhub-settings-config.yml to 'replicate the training settings of the current (2025) operational FloodHub model'. Colab tutorial loads PRE-TRAINED Google Hydrology models and computes NSE/KGE, and demonstrates fine-tuning only the static_embedding_fc layer for outlier basins.
sources.relevance: medium - the architecture and pretrained weights are genuinely the state of the art and the fine-tune-the-static-embedding trick is the cheap way to adapt a global model to one odd basin. But see the caveat: the data substrate has no Indian basins, so you cannot evaluate the pretrained model on the Periyar without building your own Caravan-format extension first. Treat it as an architecture reference and a stretch goal, not a drop-in.
sources.last_activity: pushed 2026-08-25 (very active; repo is <1 year old)
sources.download_hint: conda env create -f environments/conda.yml; conda activate googlehydrology; pip install -e . Data: Caravan NetCDF from doi 10.5281/zenodo.6522634, forcings from gs://caravan-multimet/v1.1.
sources.caveat: Data dependency is Caravan/MultiMet, which I verified contains ZERO Indian basins (see dead_ends). Adapting it to the Periyar means writing a Caravan-format extension for CAMELS-IND yourself.

sources.name: Caravan-MultiMet v1.1 (gs://caravan-multimet) - CHIRPS_GEFS forecast forcings
sources.what_it_provides: Verified by reading the public GCS JSON API and decoding zarr chunks directly. https://storage.googleapis.com/storage/v1/b/caravan-multimet/o?prefix=v1.1/&delimiter=/ returns seven prefixes: CHIRPS, CHIRPS_GEFS, CPC, ERA5_LAND, GRAPHCAST, HRES, IMERG. The CHIRPS_GEFS zarr .zmetadata gives array chirpsgefs_precipitation with shape [18655, 8797, 16] over dims ['basin','date','lead_time'], date units 'days since 1999-01-01', lead_time units 'days'. So this is a basin-aggregated, per-lead-day precipitation FORECAST archive spanning ~1999-2023 for 18,655 basins - structurally exactly what a forecast-driven hydrology model needs.
sources.relevance: low for direct use, high as a template. I decoded all four chunks of the basin coordinate array (18,656 entries) and the composition is: hysets 11420, GRDC 3485, camelsbr 895, lamah 830, camels(US) 671, camelscl 472, camelsch 296, camelses 269, camelsaus 222, il 95. Zero entries contain 'ind'. Zero GRDC station ids begin '23' (the WMO South Asia block). India is absent. But the [basin, date, lead_time] zarr layout with a matched observed-precip product is the right data model for AquaSync's own forecast archive - build the same thing for Idukki/Idamalayar from GEFS.

sources.name: CHIRPS-GEFS bias-corrected precipitation forecasts (UCSB Climate Hazards Center)
sources.what_it_provides: A true archived forecast product covering October 2021, verified by directory listing and HTTP headers. https://data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/EWX/data/forecasts/CHIRPS-GEFS_precip_v12/daily_16day/2021/10/15/ returns 200 and lists data.2021.1015.tif, data.2021.1016.tif, data.2021.1017.tif ... i.e. one GeoTIFF per forecast valid-day, issued on 2021-10-15, out to 16 days. HEAD on data.2021.1018.tif returns HTTP/1.1 200, Content-Length: 57616610, and crucially Last-Modified: Fri, 15 Oct 2021 20:52:22 GMT - proving the file was written on the issue date and is a genuine contemporaneous forecast, not a retrofit. Year directories run 2000/ through 2026/. Global 0.05 deg, GEFS precipitation bias-corrected onto the CHIRPS climatology.
sources.relevance: high as the deterministic control arm of the hindcast. It is far better resolved than raw GEFS (0.05 deg vs 0.25 deg) and already bias-corrected against a satellite/gauge blend, which matters enormously over a 30 km wide orographic gradient like the Western Ghats. Use it as the 'best available deterministic forecast' baseline against which the GEFS 30-member spread earns (or fails to earn) its keep in AquaSync's benefit accounting.

IDAMALAYAR appears as a separate labelled row. Columns present: Min.Draw Down Level, Level(m), Effective Storage (mcm), Storage %, Gen. Capability (mu), RF (mm), Spill, Inflow (mcm/day), Cum. sources.name: Sudheer et al. (2019), 'Role of dams on the floods of August 2018 in Periyar River Basin, Kerala', Current Science 116(5), 780-794
sources.what_it_provides: PDF downloaded (4,413,605 bytes, 15 pages) and text-extracted, so the following is verbatim-verified rather than second-hand. The forecast-skill passage reads: 'The probability of detection (POD) of higher rainfall (>25 mm/day) at short range (3-day) or medium range (5-day) even with the ensemble of models is still low at about 20% to 30% only[23] with a large probability of false alarm[24].' Immediately preceding: 'Though the accuracy of district level medium range rainfall forecast (up to 5-7 days in advance) is 75-85% in monsoon season, the accuracy of QPF with regards to rainfall magnitude is low.' Refs 23/24 are Durai & Bhardwaj, Geofizika 30, 119-141 (2013) and Durai, Bhardwaj, Roy Bhowmik & Rama Rao, Mausam 66, 479-496 (2015). Other quantitative results from the same paper, all directly useful to AquaSync: PRB catchment area 5398 km2; Periyar is 244 km long, regulated by 17 dams/barrages, 80% of Kerala's hydroelectric projects; Aug 2018 was a 145-year return period rainfall; only 16-21% peak attenuation at Neeleswaram was achievable even by pre-emptively emptying reservoirs (16% for 75% end-of-July storage, 21% for 50% or 25% storage); OBSERVED peak 8800 m3/s against a bank-full capacity at Neeleswaram of ~4200 m3/s (9965 m3/s in the same sentence is the HEC-HMS MODELLED peak, not observed - corrected 28 Aug 2026); probability of an August ERE of that kind in the PRB is 0.6%.
sources.relevance: high - it is the ceiling on what AquaSync may honestly claim, and it is about THIS basin. It also supplies the peer-reviewed framing for why forecast-driven operation is the right research question ('improvement in the reliability of forecasting of EREs coupled with a good inflow forecasting system could help improve the management of reservoirs') and a hard, citable upper bound on achievable peak attenuation.
sources.license: Current Science is open access; free to read and cite
sources.download_hint: https://www.currentscience.ac.in/Volumes/116/05/0780.pdf - direct, no paywall, no bot block.
sources.caveat: CORRECTION TO THE PRIOR SWEEP: the POD statement is on journal page 792, NOT page 789. Verified by per-page extraction (pdftotext -f 13 -l 13; pdf page 13 carries the running page number 792, and page 789 = pdf page 10 contains no such text). The substance of the prior sweep's claim is correct and confirmed; only the page citation is wrong. Second caveat: the 20-30% POD number is Sudheer et al. reporting OTHER people's verification (Durai 2013/2015) for INDIA AS A WHOLE, not a Periyar-specific or Western-Ghats-specific measurement, and the 2013/2015 vintage predates roughly a decade of EPS improvement. Cite it as 'the most basin-proximate published statement', not as a current measured skill for this catchment.

sources.name: Durai, Bhardwaj, Roy Bhowmik & Rama Rao (2015), 'Verification of quantitative precipitation forecasts from operational ensemble prediction systems over India', Mausam 66(3), 479-496
sources.what_it_provides: Full PDF downloaded (775,531 bytes) and text-extracted. This is the primary source behind the 'large probability of false alarm' half of the Sudheer claim, and it carries the actual numbers AquaSync needs for realistic monsoon forecast error growth. Verified content: verification of ECMWF, UKMO, NCEP and JMA EPS from the TIGGE archive over India, 1 June - 30 September 2012, all trimmed to 20 members for comparability. THE KEY NUMBER FOR THE WESTERN GHATS: 'The RMSE range between 10-15 mm over most parts of India and it is relatively higher (25-30 mm) over parts of NE India AND ALONG THE WEST COAST OF INDIA in all four EPS ensemble mean forecast' (day-3 ensemble-mean rainfall). All-India seasonal mean RMSE is 'of the order 13-14 mm/day' for all four EPS across day-1 to day-7. Spatial correlation coefficient of the ensemble mean, day-1 to day-7: ECMWF 0.4-0.5, UKMO 0.31-0.45, NCEP 0.29-0.48, JMA 0.29-0.40. Temporal CC at day-3 lies between 0.6 and 0.7 for ECMWF and NCEP members, below 0.7 for UKMO/JMA, and decreases with lead time. ACC is significant at 99% only above 0.239 (n=122 monsoon days). 'The magnitude of ACC values decreases from west coast of India to east coast of India in all the EPS forecast.' Probabilistic thresholds used: 0.1, 2.5, 7, 35, 64 mm/day. BSS is positive for all four EPS at >5 mm/day but smaller at >10 mm/day; BSS is NEGATIVE for JMA and UKMO over dry regions. ECMWF EPS has the largest ROC area at every lead time; 'as the forecast lead time goes longer, the curve is closer to the diagonal'.
sources.relevance: high - this is the requested 'actual published skill numbers' for monsoon rainfall error growth, and it is the only source found that isolates the WEST COAST as a distinct, worse-performing region. The 25-30 mm/day day-3 ensemble-mean RMSE on the west coast is the number AquaSync should quote when it explains why the forecast-driven benefit is much smaller than the perfect-foresight benefit. It also justifies choosing ECMWF ENS over the others if TIGGE is used.
sources.http_status: 200 (article landing page); 200 on the PDF at /article/download/557/483/1884
sources.last_activity: published July 2015; landing page live and serving downloads in 2026
sources.caveat: Single monsoon season (JJAS 2012) and a decade old. The scores are averaged over Indian LAND grid points, and the west-coast RMSE figure is read from the paper's descriptive text about a spatial map, not from a Periyar-specific table. Several headline curves (POD/FAR by threshold and lead day) live only in figures, so I could NOT extract per-threshold POD/FAR numbers from the text - do not invent them. The companion Geofizika 2013 paper could not be retrieved: geofizika-journal.gfz.hr returns curl code 000 (DNS/host dead) and Crossref has no record for it.

sources.name: Nitha, Pramada, Praseed & Sridhar (2025), 'Performance Evaluation of Numerical Weather Prediction Models in Forecasting Rainfall Events in Kerala, India', Atmosphere 16(4), 372
sources.what_it_provides: The most directly on-target modern reference found: a region-specific verification of SIX NWP models - NCEP, NCMRWF, ECMWF, CMA, UKMO, JMA - for heavy rainfall events over Kerala, explicitly motivated by the Western Ghats. Uses traditional metrics, categorical precipitation metrics and Fractional Skill Scores across different forecast lead times, with FSS computed at 100 mm, 50 mm and 5 mm thresholds. Verified findings from the abstract: 'all models captured rainfall patterns well for the lower threshold of 5 mm, but most of the models struggled to accurately forecast heavy rainfall, especially for longer lead times'; JMA scored well on most metrics but had HIGH False Alarm Ratio; ECMWF 'demonstrated consistent performance'; NCEP and UKMO moderate; CMA and NCMRWF lowest accuracy.
sources.relevance: high - it is 2025, it is Kerala, it is the Western Ghats, it is heavy-rainfall thresholds, and its qualitative conclusion independently corroborates Sudheer's 2019 warning with modern models. It is the best available citation for 'heavy-rainfall skill over this basin is still poor at longer lead times' without relying on 2013-vintage numbers.

sources.name: Nearing et al. (2024), 'Global prediction of extreme floods in ungauged watersheds', Nature 627(8004), 559-563
sources.what_it_provides: Citation verified identical across Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Europe PMC: Nature 627(8004), 559-563, published 20 March 2024, 18 authors (Nearing, Cohen, Dube, Gauch, Gilon, Harrigan, Hassidim, Klotz, Kratzert, Metzger, Nevo, Pappenberger, Prudhomme, Shalev, Shenzis, Tekalign, Weitzner, Matias), PMID 38509278, PMCID PMC10954541. Headline results quoted from the open-access full text: 'Compared with GloFAS nowcasts (0-day lead time), AI forecasts have either better or not statistically different reliability (F1 scores) up to a 5-day lead time for 1-year (N = 2,415, P = 6x10^-6, d = 0.08), 2-year (P = 0.98, d = 2x10^-4) and 5-year (P = 0.69, d = 0.025) return period events.' AI at a 5-year return period matches GloFAS at a 1-year return period on precision and beats it on recall (P = 1x10^-18, d = 0.20). The nowcast beats GloFAS v4 at 64%/70%/60%/49% of gauges for 1/2/5/10-year events (at least equivalent at 65%/73%/73%/76%). Absolute F1 ranges: GloFAS 0.15 (South America) to 0.32 (Europe); AI 0.21 (South America) to 0.46 (Southwest Pacific). Trained on 5,680 gauges / 152,259 gauge-years; skill mapped over 1.03 million HydroBASINS level-12 watersheds; operational in 'over 80 countries'.
sources.relevance: medium - it is the citation of record for the model behind GRRR and Flood Hub, and it establishes that a global ML model can beat a calibrated global physical model at ungauged locations, which is the intellectual licence for AquaSync to use a GRRR virtual gauge near Idukki at all. But see the caveat: it says nothing whatsoever about India, so it cannot be cited as evidence of skill on the Periyar.

sources.caveat: VERIFIED NEGATIVE, and it matters: a full-text search of the Europe PMC XML (abstract, main text, all captions, Methods, availability statements) finds 'India' 0, 'Indian' 0, 'Kerala' 0, 'Periyar' 0, 'Ganges' 0, 'Brahmaputra' 0, 'Bangladesh' 0, 'Nepal' 0, 'Pakistan' 0, 'South Asia' 0. 'Asia' appears exactly twice and both are the SAME NULL RESULT: Asia is one of only three exceptions where the AI model is not statistically distinguishable from GloFAS, at 5-year (P = 0.04, d = 0.12) and 10-year (P = 0.18, d = 0.12) return periods - i.e. for exactly the large events AquaSync cares about, on exactly this continent, the headline advantage does not hold. Note also: the paper reports NO percentage improvement in precision or recall (effect sizes are Cohen's d only), so any 'X% better precision' attributed to it is fabricated; the authors state 'the comparison favours the GloFAS benchmark' because GloFAS could only be benchmarked at 0-day lead; and there is a genuine internal inconsistency, with the main text saying 5,680 training gauges and Extended Data Fig. 6 saying 5,860.

technologies.name: Ensemble-forecast-driven reservoir policy search (GEFS members -> existing SCS-CN/Muskingum chain -> existing exhaustive policy search)
technologies.limitations: Cost is 30x the current single-trajectory policy evaluation, which matters because AquaSync's search is already exhaustive over (target level, start hour, max rate). Requires a decision rule over the ensemble - expected value, CVaR, or a regret-minimising choice - and that rule choice materially changes the answer, so it must be stated, not buried. GEFS 0.25 deg cannot resolve the Western Ghats orographic gradient and will be biased low over the escarpment, so an uncorrected run understates inflow and will make the forecast-driven policy look worse than a bias-corrected one honestly would.
technologies.recent_updates: GEFSv12 has been operational since 2020-09-23, so October 2021 is the same model generation running today - skill measured on the 2021 hindcast transfers to present-day operations, which is a genuinely strong argument for the case study.
technologies.fit_for_aquasync: This is THE recommendation and it closes the stated gap with components that already exist. Concretely: (1) for each 00z issue date across the Oct 2021 event, range-fetch APCP for gep01..gep30 out to 240 h over the Periyar cells; (2) bias-correct member precipitation against IMD 0.25 deg gridded rainfall or the SLDC daily RF column; (3) push each member through the existing SCS-CN + Muskingum chain to get 30 inflow trajectories; (4) run the existing exhaustive policy search per member and pick a policy by a declared rule; (5) evaluate the CHOSEN policy against the TRUE observed inflow from the SLDC scrape. The deliverable is a single honest number - the fraction of the perfect-foresight benefit that survives - plus its decay with lead time. Report it at 24/72/120 h separately, because the literature says those are very different regimes.

technologies.name: GRRR reforecast as a ready-made ML inflow hindcast (no model training required)
technologies.limitations: It is a REFORECAST run with a modern model, not the forecast that was operationally issued in October 2021, so it is optimistic relative to what an operator actually had - it must be labelled as an upper-middle bound, not as 'the forecast available at the time'. Lead time stops at 7 days and the axis stops at 2023-06-30, so it cannot support live operation. The gauge is a HydroBASINS level-12 VIRTUAL outlet (hybas_4121152880, 0.61 km from Idukki dam), a modelled point never calibrated against Idukki's measured inflow, and its discharge is total routed streamflow at a basin outlet rather than reservoir inflow per se. Its magnitudes need checking against the SLDC scrape before any use.
technologies.recent_updates: Public as model_id_8583a5c2_v0; reanalysis 1980-01-01 to 2023-12-23, reforecast 2016-01-01 to 2023-06-30 at 0-7 day lead (lead 0 = reanalysis, not a forecast - see the source-level note on this bucket); CC BY 4.0 with the licence file in the bucket; readable anonymously with no key or waitlist.
technologies.fit_for_aquasync: Very good, and it is the cheapest single win available - it requires zero model training and zero GRIB decoding, just an xarray.open_zarr with token='anon'. The highest-value use is as the SECOND arm of a three-way comparison for October 2021: (a) perfect foresight, which is what AquaSync reports today; (b) GRRR reforecast inflow at 1, 3, 5 and 7 day lead, which is 'a good modern ML forecast'; (c) the 30-member GEFS ensemble pushed through AquaSync's own SCS-CN/Muskingum chain, which is 'what actually existed in 2021'. The gap between (a) and (c) is the headline honesty correction; the gap between (b) and (c) tells the project how much of its loss is attributable to its own rainfall-runoff model rather than to atmospheric predictability. Do (a)-(c) first if time is short; add (b) because it is nearly free.

technologies.name: LSTM rainfall-runoff / inflow forecasting via NeuralHydrology on CAMELS-IND
technologies.limitations: Single-basin LSTMs are the weak form of the method and often lose to a well-calibrated conceptual model; the published advantage comes from pooling many basins. CAMELS-IND streamflow at Neeleswaram is a REGULATED series downstream of Idukki and Idamalayar, so a model trained on it learns dam operating behaviour as much as hydrology. CAMELS-IND ends 2020-12-31, so October 2021 is outside the dataset entirely and must come from the SLDC scrape. Forcings are IMD/IMDAA gridded, which have their own orographic biases in exactly this terrain.
technologies.recent_updates: v1.13.0 released 2026-01-14; repo pushed 2026-08-09; datasetzoo/camelsind.py makes CAMELS-IND first-class; four forecast-sequence LSTM architectures and CMAL/UMAL/GMM probabilistic heads are in the model zoo.
technologies.fit_for_aquasync: Good but SECOND priority behind the ensemble hindcast, because it does not by itself remove perfect foresight - it replaces one deterministic inflow estimate with another unless you use the probabilistic heads and forecast-sequence architectures. The high-value version is: pool the 32 CAMELS-IND basin-15 catchments (or all 472) to pretrain, fine-tune on Vandiperiyar (712 km2, the unregulated headwater proxy for Idukki's catchment), use a handoff_forecast_lstm with GEFS members as the forecast-sequence forcing and a CMAL head, and you get a calibrated predictive DISTRIBUTION of inflow. That is a genuinely stronger object than 30 raw member trajectories. It is also a multi-week piece of work.

technologies.name: OpenHydroNet / Google Flood Hub model architectures (Mean-Embedding-Forecast-LSTM)
technologies.limitations: Its data substrate, Caravan/MultiMet, contains zero Indian basins (verified by decoding the full 18,656-entry basin index). The pretrained weights therefore have never seen an Indian catchment, and there is no in-distribution basin to validate against near the Periyar. Adapting means writing a Caravan-format extension for CAMELS-IND first. The repo is under a year old and explicitly 'not an officially supported Google product'.
technologies.recent_updates: Repo created 2025-09-29, 328 stars, pushed 2026-08-25. Production Flood Hub model as of December 2025 is the Mean-Embedding-Forecast-LSTM (Gauch et al., HESS 29, 6221, 2025). Colab tutorial demonstrates fine-tuning only static_embedding_fc for outlier basins - the cheap adaptation path.
technologies.fit_for_aquasync: Reference architecture, not a dependency. The one idea worth stealing immediately and cheaply is the hindcast/forecast sequence SPLIT - a model that ingests observed forcing up to the issue time and NWP forcing beyond it, with separate embeddings. That is the correct inductive bias for exactly AquaSync's problem and it is available in plain NeuralHydrology too. Do not make the project's critical path depend on getting Google's pretrained weights to work on a basin they have never seen.

technologies.name: Physics-informed neural networks and learned surrogates for hydraulics
technologies.limitations: Independent reviews converge on the same verdict: PINNs for the shallow-water/Saint-Venant equations are 'still in its exploratory phase', with loss-term balancing problems, hard and long training, accuracy still BELOW conventional numerical solvers, and poor transferability across catchments and hydroclimatic regimes. Reference implementations are research code: maziarraissi/PINNs 6114 stars but last pushed 2026-02-11; lululxvi/deepxde 4389 stars, LGPL-2.1, pushed 2026-08-18; NVIDIA/physicsnemo-sym 335 stars, pushed 2026-04-28.
technologies.recent_updates: 2024-2026 work on coupled 1D sewer / 2D surface PINNs and on PINN+MPC for computing optimal dam floodgate signals; conditional latent-dynamics surrogates of the shallow-water equations for metropolitan flood digital twins.
technologies.fit_for_aquasync: NO. The surrogate argument only pays when the physics model is the bottleneck - hours per city-scale hydraulic run. AquaSync's forward model is a level-storage power law plus SCS-CN plus Muskingum; it is already effectively instantaneous, which is precisely why an EXHAUSTIVE policy search is feasible at all. Replacing a millisecond analytic model with a neural surrogate that is slower to train, less accurate, and harder to defend would be strictly negative value. The single exception worth noting for a future phase: if AquaSync ever adds 2D downstream inundation mapping below Neeleswaram, that IS the regime where a surrogate earns its keep. Not now.

technologies.name: Digital twin platforms (Eclipse Ditto, NVIDIA Omniverse/PhysicsNeMo, Azure Digital Twins)
technologies.limitations: All three are real, maintained products - Eclipse Ditto 920 stars, EPL-2.0, pushed 2026-08-27; NVIDIA/physicsnemo 3203 stars, Apache-2.0, pushed 2026-08-27; Azure Digital Twins is a paid managed service. None of them solves a problem AquaSync has. Ditto is a device-shadow/state-synchronisation layer for fleets of IoT things - AquaSync has two reservoirs and one river, not ten thousand devices. Azure Digital Twins adds a DTDL modelling layer, a cloud bill, vendor lock-in and an operational surface, in exchange for a graph abstraction over a system with about five nodes. Omniverse/PhysicsNeMo is a GPU physics-ML and 3D visualisation stack aimed at CFD-scale surrogates.
technologies.recent_updates: All actively developed as of 2026-08. NVIDIA Modulus was renamed PhysicsNeMo (github.com/NVIDIA/modulus now 301-redirects).
technologies.fit_for_aquasync: NO, for all three, and the honest answer should be stated plainly in the report rather than hedged. 'Digital twin' in AquaSync's title is a description of what the model DOES - a calibrated, replayable representation of a physical system driven by real data - not a mandate to adopt a product with that phrase in its marketing. Adopting any of these would add infrastructure, cost and a dependency without improving a single number in the results, and would consume effort that belongs on the forecast-uncertainty gap. The one component in this family that could matter later is PhysicsNeMo, and only if the project moves to GPU-scale 2D hydraulics.

technologies.name: Reservoir inflow forecasting for Indian dams (published baselines)
technologies.limitations: The Indian literature is thin, mostly single-reservoir, and almost entirely AUTOREGRESSIVE - it forecasts inflow from past inflow rather than from a rainfall forecast, which means it cannot answer AquaSync's question at all. The closest paper to this basin, Skariah & Suriyakala (2022), Arabian Journal of Geosciences 15, doi 10.1007/s12517-022-10564-x (DOI verified 200, 8 citations), forecasts Idukki reservoir inflow comparing exponential smoothing, ARIMA and LSTM, but uses only daily data from 2015-2020 and is paywalled. Other Indian work covers Hirakud (LSTM/stacked/bidirectional variants), Bhakra (~20 years daily) and Sri Ram Sagar in Telangana (Bi-LSTM, 2024).
technologies.recent_updates: 2024-2025 work on multi-head attention for daily inflow with flood-peak emphasis, and on hybrid hydrologic-hydrodynamic-deep-learning for the dam-regulated Mahanadi delta.
technologies.fit_for_aquasync: Useful as a LOW BAR to clear and as evidence of a real gap in the literature, not as a method to copy. There is an Idukki-specific published baseline (Skariah & Suriyakala 2022) that AquaSync can position against, and the fact that it is autoregressive on 6 years of data means an NWP-forced, ensemble-driven, 41-year-trained forecast for the same reservoir is a defensible contribution rather than a re-run. Do NOT quote the MAPE figure that circulates in secondary summaries of that paper - I could not verify it against the paper text.

key_findings: THE GAP IS CLOSEABLE, AND EXACTLY ONE SOURCE CLOSES IT. NOAA GEFS on AWS (s3://noaa-gefs-pds) holds full 30-member ensemble precipitation forecasts for October 2021 over the Periyar, free and unauthenticated. Verified concretely: gefs.20211015/00/atmos/pgrb2sp25/ contains gep01 through gep30 at f000-f240, the .idx sidecar names 'APCP:surface:18-24 hour acc fcst:ENS=+1' at byte offset 8942680, and a Range GET of that slice returned HTTP 206, 268556 bytes, starting with the magic word GRIB. AquaSync can therefore replay October 2021 with the forecast that genuinely existed at the time, run its existing policy search on 30 error-bearing inflow trajectories instead of one perfect one, and report what fraction of the claimed benefit survives.

A SECOND, INDEPENDENT ROUTE EXISTS, AND IT IS DISCHARGE RATHER THAN RAINFALL. Google's GRRR (Runoff Reanalysis & Reforecast) sits in an anonymously readable GCS bucket, gs://flood-forecasting/hydrologic_predictions/model_id_8583a5c2_v0/, with no key and no waitlist. Its reforecast/streamflow.zarr is [1,031,646 gauges x 2,738 issue times x 8 lead times], contiguous 2016-01-01 to 2023-06-30 at 0-7 day lead - so it spans October 2021. Kerala is covered: 589 virtual gauges in the Kerala bbox, 96 in the Periyar catchment box, and hybas_4121152880 sits 0.61 km from Idukki dam. Its reanalysis reproduces the August 2018 flood (peak 239.65 m3/s on 2018-08-16) against its own return-period thresholds of 173.2 / 214.9 / 242.2 m3/s at 2 / 5 / 10 years. Running this ALONGSIDE the GEFS rainfall hindcast is what lets AquaSync separate 'the rainfall forecast was wrong' from 'my rainfall-runoff model was wrong' - two error sources it currently cannot tell apart.

EVERY OTHER FREE ENSEMBLE ROUTE FAILS THE 2021 HINDCAST TEST, AND EACH FAILURE WAS MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED. Open-Meteo's ensemble endpoint answers a 2021 request with "Parameter 'start_date' is out of allowed range from 2026-05-26 to 2026-10-01" - a ~3-month member window. ECMWF Open Data retains about 4 days at data.ecmwf.int and its AWS mirror's earliest prefix is 20230118. The GEFSv12 REFORECAST bucket stops at 2020, one year short. CHIRPS-GEFS does reach back to 2000 but ships only the bias-corrected ensemble MEAN. TIGGE (2006-10-01 to present, 13 centres, 12-51 members) is the only alternative that works, and it now requires the new ECDS API after a 2026-05-27 migration that invalidated most published recipes.

A TRAP THAT WOULD HAVE SILENTLY FAKED THE HINDCAST. Open-Meteo's Historical Forecast API cheerfully returns hourly precipitation for October 2021 and looks like a hindcast. It is not one. Requesting the lead-time variable precipitation_previous_day3 for 2021-10-15 returns 24 nulls; the same request for 2024-07-15 returns 24 real values. Probing 2021-07, 2022-01, 2022-07, 2023-01, 2023-07 and 2024-01 gave all nulls, while 2024-04-15 and 2024-06-01 gave data - so the lead-time archive begins in early 2024. For 2021 that API serves what is effectively an analysis, i.e. a near-perfect-foresight field. Building the 'forecast-driven' comparison on it would reproduce the perfect-foresight result while appearing to have fixed it.

THE PRIOR SWEEP'S SUDHEER CLAIM IS CORRECT IN SUBSTANCE AND WRONG IN ITS PAGE NUMBER. The PDF was downloaded and text-extracted. The sentence reads exactly: 'The probability of detection (POD) of higher rainfall (>25 mm/day) at short range (3-day) or medium range (5-day) even with the ensemble of models is still low at about 20% to 30% only with a large probability of false alarm.' It sits on journal page 792, not 789 (verified by per-page extraction; page 789 is pdf page 10 and contains no such text). Two further qualifications matter for honest reporting: the 20-30% figure is Sudheer et al. quoting other people's ALL-INDIA verification (Durai & Bhardwaj 2013; Durai et al. 2015), not a Periyar-specific measurement, and those studies are 2013/2015 vintage.

ABSOLUTE RAINFALL FORECAST ERRORS OVER THE WESTERN GHATS ARE ROUGHLY DOUBLE THE ALL-INDIA VALUE - BECAUSE THE RAINFALL ITSELF IS ROUGHLY DOUBLE, NOT BECAUSE SKILL IS WORSE THERE. CORRECTED 28 Aug 2026 after adversarial verification found the original framing inverted its own source. Durai et al. (2015), Mausam 66(3) 479-496, full PDF retrieved: day-3 ensemble-mean rainfall RMSE is 10-15 mm/day over most of India but 25-30 mm/day 'along the west coast of India' and over NE India, in all four of ECMWF, UKMO, NCEP and JMA EPS - but this is an ABSOLUTE error, and the same paper gives an observed seasonal mean of 'about 15 mm/day over Konkan coast', i.e. RMSE is largest exactly where rainfall is largest. The paper's actual SKILL metric says the opposite: 'The magnitude of ACC values decreases from west coast of India to east coast of India in all the EPS forecast' - the west coast has the HIGHEST anomaly correlation of any region, in every one of the four EPS. All-India seasonal RMSE is 13-14 mm/day across day-1 to day-7. Temporal CC at day-3 is 0.6-0.7 for the best members and falls with lead time; BSS at >10 mm/day is materially worse than at >5 mm/day. Nitha et al. (2025), Atmosphere 16(4) 372, is consistent with this once read in full: over Kerala at day 1-3 (its only lead times; JJAS 2018-2022 only, so it excludes October and cannot speak to the 3-7 day window this project needs) the models score CSI 0.49-0.57 with ECMWF FAR 0.41 - not a catastrophic regime, and it does not corroborate a claim about 'longer lead times' since day 3 is the longest it measures. The defensible statement AquaSync can make: forecast error over this basin is large in absolute terms because the rainfall is large, and skill decays with lead time exactly as it does everywhere else in the EPS record - not that this basin is uniquely hard to forecast.

CAMELS-IND EXISTS, COVERS KERALA, AND CONTAINS THE PERIYAR - which is not the answer the geography would suggest, since Kerala's rivers are intra-state and easy to miss. Verified by reading the Zenodo ZIP central directory over HTTP Range requests: CWC basin 15 ('West flowing rivers from Tadri to Kanyakumari') supplies 32 of the 472 catchments, ~21 of them inside Kerala, including 15021 Neeleswaram on the Periyar (10.1833 N, 76.5000 E, 4234 km2, streamflow present for 94.57% of 1980-2020, in the streamflow-sufficient subset) and 15031 Vandiperiyar (9.5733 N, 77.0908 E, 712 km2, 43.51%). Daily forcings run 1980-01-01 to 2020-12-31 with 19 IMD/IMDAA variables. NeuralHydrology already ships datasetzoo/camelsind.py, so this is loadable without writing an adapter. Use v2.2 (10.5281/zenodo.14999580), not the v2.1 DOI the ESSD paper cites - the v2.2 changelog specifically corrects 'the gauge_id mapping for basin codes 12 and 15', and 15 is this basin.

THE KERALA SLDC FORM SERVES ARBITRARY HISTORICAL DATES, which the prior sweep had identified as a source but not established as usable for 2021. POST to https://sldckerala.com/index.php?id=7 with body 'date1_day=15&date1_month=10&date1_year=2021&sbtstore=SHOW' returns a page headed 'STORAGE AS ON 15.10.2021' with the row IDUKKI | 728.813 m | 1261.034 mcm | 86% | 1.2 mm RF | 15.219 mcm/day inflow | 264.292 MU cumulative, and a separate IDAMALAYAR row. The month field must be NUMERIC - posting 'October' returns nothing, and the hidden txtDate epoch field on the page is a decoy that just returns today. This is the ground truth against which any GEFS-driven inflow forecast must be scored, and it is what makes the honest benefit-retention number computable at all.

GOOGLE'S OPEN-SOURCED FLOOD MODELS ARE REAL AND CURRENT, BUT THEIR TRAINING DATA HAS NEVER SEEN INDIA. google-research/flood-forecasting ('OpenHydroNet', 328 stars, Apache-2.0, created 2025-09-29, pushed 2026-08-25) is a fork of NeuralHydrology implementing the actual December-2025 production Flood Hub architecture. Its data substrate is Caravan/MultiMet - and decoding all four chunks of the 18,656-entry basin index gives hysets 11420, GRDC 3485, camelsbr 895, lamah 830, camels(US) 671, camelscl 472, camelsch 296, camelses 269, camelsaus 222, il 95, with zero ids containing 'ind' and zero GRDC stations in the '23' South Asia block. India is absent from the training set even though India is a supported Flood Hub country, so the pretrained weights have no in-distribution Indian basin to validate against.

THE NATURE 2024 PAPER CANNOT BE CITED AS EVIDENCE OF SKILL IN INDIA, AND ITS ONE ASIA RESULT IS A NULL RESULT. A full-text search of the open-access Europe PMC XML of Nearing et al. (Nature 627(8004), 559-563) returns zero occurrences of India, Indian, Kerala, Periyar, Ganges, Brahmaputra, Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan or South Asia. 'Asia' appears exactly twice, both reporting the same thing: Asia is one of only three exceptions where the AI model is NOT statistically distinguishable from GloFAS, at 5-year (P = 0.04, d = 0.12) and 10-year (P = 0.18, d = 0.12) return periods - precisely the large events AquaSync exists to handle. The paper also reports no percentage improvement in precision or recall (Cohen's d only), so any 'X% better' figure attributed to it is invented, and it carries a real internal inconsistency (5,680 training gauges in the main text versus 5,860 in Extended Data Fig. 6). The case for using GRRR on the Periyar rests on the supported-countries list and on the GRRR data itself, not on this paper.

THE MOST VALUABLE STRUCTURE FOUND IS NOT A MODEL BUT A DATA LAYOUT. Caravan-MultiMet stores its forecast forcing as a zarr array of shape [basin, date, lead_time] - specifically chirpsgefs_precipitation [18655, 8797, 16] with lead_time in days. That is the right shape for AquaSync's own forecast archive: build [issue_date, lead_hour, member] arrays of basin-mean precipitation for Idukki and Idamalayar from the GEFS range reads, and every downstream question - error growth with lead time, ensemble spread versus error, benefit retention by lead - becomes a slice rather than a re-scrape.

NO DIGITAL TWIN PLATFORM IS WORTH ADOPTING HERE, AND SAYING SO IS THE FINDING. Eclipse Ditto (920 stars, EPL-2.0, pushed 2026-08-27), Azure Digital Twins and NVIDIA Omniverse/PhysicsNeMo (3203 stars, Apache-2.0, pushed 2026-08-27) are all healthy, maintained products aimed at problems AquaSync does not have: device-shadow synchronisation across large IoT fleets, a DTDL graph over many-noded assets, and GPU physics-ML at CFD scale. AquaSync is two reservoirs, one river and an analytic forward model. Similarly, PINN surrogates for the shallow-water equations are still 'in an exploratory phase' with accuracy below conventional solvers - and AquaSync's physics is already instantaneous, which is the only reason its exhaustive policy search is tractable. Replacing it with a slower, less accurate learned surrogate would be strictly negative value.

THE HONEST HEADLINE THE PROJECT SHOULD AIM FOR. Sudheer et al. (2019) found that for the August 2018 event, even pre-emptively emptying Periyar reservoirs to 25-50% capacity bought only 16-21% peak attenuation at Neeleswaram, against an OBSERVED peak of 8800 m3/s (9965 m3/s is Sudheer et al.'s HEC-HMS MODELLED peak, from the same sentence - corrected 28 Aug 2026 after verification caught the two numbers transposed) and a bank-full capacity of ~4200 m3/s - and they explicitly named forecast reliability at 3-7 day lead as the binding constraint. Combined with the 25-30 mm/day day-3 west-coast RMSE, the defensible claim for AquaSync is not 'X% benefit' but 'X% under perfect foresight, Y% with the 30-member GEFS ensemble that was actually available, decaying from 24 h to 120 h as follows'. That framing turns the project's biggest methodological weakness into its most credible result.

Open-Meteo Historical Forecast API as a lead-time hindcast. It returns data for October 2021 and therefore looks like it works. It does not: precipitation_previous_day3 is 100% null for 2021-10-15 (0 of 24 hours populated) while identical for 2024-07-15 gives 24 of 24. ECMWF Open Data for October 2021. data.ecmwf.int/forecasts/ listed exactly four date directories (20260824-20260827), roughly a 4-day rolling retention. The AWS Open Data mirror ecmwf-forecasts is deeper but its earliest prefix is 20230118/. There is no path to 2021 ECMWF ensembles here; TIGGE is the only route.

NOAA GEFSv12 REFORECAST (s3://noaa-gefs-retrospective) for October 2021. The bucket is real and returns 200, and GEFSv12/reforecast/ contains year prefixes - but they run 2000 through 2020 and stop. It misses the flagship case study by one year. The OPERATIONAL archive s3://noaa-gefs-pds (earliest prefix gefs.20170101/) is the one that covers 2021.

Caravan / Caravan-MultiMet as a source of Indian training or evaluation basins. Decoded all four blosc chunks of the basin coordinate array: 18,656 entries, composition hysets 11420 / GRDC 3485 / camelsbr 895 / lamah 830 / camels 671 / camelscl 472 / camelsch 296 / camelses 269 / camelsaus 222 / il 95. Zero ids contain 'ind'; zero GRDC station ids start with the '23' South Asia block. India is simply absent, so Google's pretrained OpenHydroNet weights have no in-distribution Indian basin and cannot be evaluated on the Periyar without you first building a Caravan-format CAMELS-IND extension.

CHIRPS-GEFS as an ensemble source. The archive is excellent and genuinely reaches October 2021 with contemporaneous Last-Modified timestamps, but listing the entire CHIRPS-GEFS_precip_v12 tree shows only aggregation-period directories (daily_16day, 05day, 10day, 15day, pentad, dekad) and no per-member directory. It is the bias-corrected ensemble MEAN only. Useful as the deterministic control arm; it cannot supply spread.

IMD's own NWP portal as a data source. nwp.imd.gov.in returns 200 but is a LOGIN WALL - the page body says only 'These are Numerical Weather Prediction models guidance. For final forecast kindly see the Bulletin and Warning issued by IMD' with no product listing, no formats, no archive, and nothing downloadable unauthenticated. www.ncmrwf.gov.in returns curl code 000 (host unreachable) though rds.ncmrwf.gov.in returns 200. indiawris.gov.in/wris/ returns 000 and ssl.imdpune.gov.in/nwp_ensemble/ returns 000. Plan on international products (GEFS/TIGGE) for forecasts and IMD gridded rainfall only for observed truth.

Google Flood Forecasting API as a route to an October 2021 hindcast. The endpoint is live and gated (403 PERMISSION_DENIED without a key), India IS on the 154-country supported list, and the method surface was fully mapped with a 403-vs-404 oracle - but the reference docs impose a hard archive floor: queryGaugeForecasts says of issuedTimeStart 'Start time cannot be earlier than 2023-10-01', and floodStatus says 'The minimum allowed cutoff time is 2025-08-01T00:00:00Z'. October 2021 is permanently unreachable through the API. Access also needs waitlist approval that Google warns 'might take several months'. Use GRRR (no key, no waitlist, covers 2016-2023) for the historical work instead.

Enumerating Flood Hub gauges from the public web frontend. sites.research.google/floods/ returns 200 (776 KB) but is a Google BOQ/Wiz application: gauge markers are not JSON but signed Google Maps MDB vector tile layers, and dynamic data goes through BOQ batchexecute. Tried and failed: /floods/_/FloodsDataHubUi/data/batchexecute returns 405 on GET and 400 on POST across 15 different rpcids; /floods/api/gauges, /floods/gauges and /floods/_/FloodsDataHubUi/data all return 404; robots.txt and sitemap.xml return 404; the deep-link /floods/l/9.845/76.972/10 returns 200 but carries zero gauge data server-side (grep for 'hybas_' finds nothing - fully client-rendered). There is no unauthenticated gauge-listing endpoint. Go to the GRRR bucket, which exposes the same virtual-gauge geometry openly.

Durai & Bhardwaj (2013), Geofizika 30, 119-141 - the primary source Sudheer cites for the 20-30% POD figure. Not retrievable: geofizika-journal.gfz.hr returns curl code 000 (host/DNS dead), guessed PDF paths under that host also 000, hrcak.srce.hr/115172 resolves to an unrelated Croatian soil-science article, and Crossref returns no matching record for the title. The companion Durai et al. (2015) Mausam paper IS fully retrievable and carries the quantitative material, so use that instead.

Extracting numeric skill scores from Nitha et al. (2025), Atmosphere 16(4) 372. MDPI 403s every headless route: doi.org redirect, the article HTML, and /pdf, all with a browser User-Agent. Unpaywall confirms Gold OA / CC-BY but lists NO alternative mirror (url_for_pdf is null for all three OA locations). Existence, authors, venue and abstract were confirmed via the Semantic Scholar Graph API and DOAJ. The per-threshold POD/FAR/FSS numbers exist in the paper but require a real browser to lift - do not attribute numbers to it without doing that.

Zenodo via naive curl. zenodo.org/records/... returns 403 to a plain 'Mozilla/5.0' UA, and the HTML page returns a 582-byte JavaScript 'Checking your browser' interstitial even when it returns 200. The fix is not to give up: use the REST API at zenodo.org/api/records/<id> with a full Chrome UA and 'Accept: application/json', which returns 200. Separate gotcha that looks like a bot block but is not - /api/records/14005378/files returns 403 purely because Zenodo only exposes files for the LATEST version, and 14005378 (v2.1) is superseded by 14999580 (v2.2), whose /files returns 200.

Physics-informed neural networks and learned surrogates as a way to speed up AquaSync's forward model. There is nothing to speed up - the level-storage power law, SCS-CN and Muskingum are effectively instantaneous, which is exactly why the exhaustive policy search is feasible. The literature is also unambiguous that PINN accuracy for shallow-water problems is still below conventional numerical methods, with hard training and poor cross-catchment transfer. Revisit only if the project adds 2D downstream inundation mapping.

Eclipse Ditto, Azure Digital Twins and NVIDIA Omniverse as 'the digital twin platform' for AquaSync. All three are alive and well maintained (verified: Ditto 920 stars pushed 2026-08-27; physicsnemo 3203 stars pushed 2026-08-27; Azure Digital Twins pricing page 200). None addresses a problem this project has, and adopting one would add cost, lock-in and operational surface without moving a single reported number. Note also that github.com/NVIDIA/modulus now 301-redirects - the project was renamed PhysicsNeMo, and docs.nvidia.com/physicsnemo/ returns 404, so cite the GitHub repo rather than that docs path.

The MAPE figure circulating in secondary summaries of Skariah & Suriyakala (2022) for Idukki inflow. The DOI (10.1007/s12517-022-10564-x) verifies at 200 and Semantic Scholar confirms the title, authors, venue (Arabian Journal of Geosciences 15, 2022) and 8 citations, but the abstract is elided by the publisher and the paper is paywalled. The specific error number could not be verified against the paper text - cite the paper as an Idukki-specific baseline, not the number.

Citing the Nature 2024 flood paper as support for Indian or Kerala performance. Verified negative by full-text search of the Europe PMC XML: zero mentions of India, Kerala, Periyar or South Asia, and the sole Asia-specific finding is a NULL result at 5- and 10-year return periods. The Zenodo record for its data/code (10.5281/zenodo.10397664) also 403s to bots, though DataCite confirms it is live.

CORRECTED 28 Aug 2026 - THIS WAS THE MOST COSTLY WRONG REJECTION IN THE SWEEP, found by adversarial verification and then independently reconfirmed by actually building the fetcher. IMD's gridded rainfall NetCDF page IS scriptable: POST RF25=<year> to https://www.imdpune.gov.in/cmpg/Griddata/RF25.php (not a GET, and not the .html page - that only carries the form) returns HTTP 200, Content-Disposition 'attachment; filename=RF25/ind<year>_rfp25.nc', and a valid classic-NetCDF payload (magic bytes 'CDF'). scripts/acquire.py's acquire_imd_rf25 fetches 2018-2021 this way - 4/4 years, ~25.4 MB each, no login, no format converter needed. This is IMD's own gauge-based product, the canonical observed-rainfall field that IMD, CAMELS-IND, Durai et al. and Nitha et al. all validate against - a stronger bias-correction truth than the ERA5 reanalysis via Open-Meteo this dead_end originally recommended as the fallback. Use IMD RF25 as the primary truth field; keep ERA5 only as a cross-check.
